title: 542. Sets, Logic, Reasoning & Proof: Checking Truth of First-Order Statements on Finite Models
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: A universal statement with a counterexample
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a universal statement in a finite model.
questions.question: A model has domain \(\{2,4,6,7\}\), and \(E(x)\) means "\(x\) is even". Is \(\forall x\,E(x)\) true in this model?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because most elements of the domain are even.

questions.explanation: A universal statement is true in a model only when the property holds for every element of the domain. Here \(E(7)\) is false, so \(\forall x\,E(x)\) is false. One counterexample is enough.
questions.hint: Test the property on each element of the domain.

questions.concept: An existential statement with a witness
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate an existential statement in a finite model.
questions.question: A model has domain \(\{1,3,5,8\}\), and \(E(x)\) means "\(x\) is even". Is \(\exists x\,E(x)\) true in this model?

options.label: B
options.text: No, because three of the four elements are odd.

questions.explanation: An existential statement is true in a model when at least one element of the domain has the property. Since \(E(8)\) is true, the statement holds. The other elements do not matter.
questions.hint: Search the domain for one element with the property.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a statement with a universal and an existential quantifier in a finite model.
questions.question: A model has domain \(\{1,2,3\}\) with the usual order. Is \(\forall x\,\exists y\,(x<y)\) true in this model?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because \(y=x+1\) is always greater than \(x\).

options.label: B
options.text: No, because for \(x=3\) no element \(y\) of the domain satisfies \(3<y\).

questions.explanation: For \(x=1\) and \(x=2\) a larger element exists, but for \(x=3\) there is none in the domain: the number \(4\) is not available. So the statement is false in this model, although it is true in the integers.
questions.hint: The witness \(y\) must be chosen from the domain of the model.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a statement with an existential and a universal quantifier in a finite model.
questions.question: A model has domain \(\{1,2,3\}\) with the usual order. Is \(\exists x\,\forall y\,(x\le y)\) true in this model?

options.label: B
options.text: No, because no element is less than itself.

questions.explanation: The statement asks for one element that is less than or equal to every element of the domain. Taking \(x=1\) works: \(1\le 1\), \(1\le 2\), and \(1\le 3\). The case \(y=x\) causes no difficulty, because \(\le\) allows equality.
questions.hint: Look for a single element that works for all choices of \(y\).

questions.learningObjective: Compare two statements that differ only in the order of their quantifiers.
questions.question: A model has domain \(\{1,2,3\}\). Which statement is true in this model?
questions.explanation: For each \(x\) there is a different element \(y\), so \(\forall x\,\exists y\,(x\ne y)\) is true. The second statement asks for a single \(y\) that differs from every \(x\), including \(x=y\), which is impossible. Exchanging the order of the quantifiers changes the meaning.
questions.hint: In the second statement, the same \(y\) must work for every \(x\), including \(x=y\).

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a quantified statement about a relation listed as pairs.
questions.question: A model has domain \(\{a,b,c\}\) and a relation \(L=\{(a,b),(b,c),(c,a)\}\). Is \(\forall x\,\exists y\,L(x,y)\) true in this model?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes; \(a\) is related to \(b\), \(b\) to \(c\), and \(c\) to \(a\).

options.label: B
options.text: No; no element is related to itself.

questions.explanation: The statement requires each element to be the first component of at least one pair of \(L\). The pairs \((a,b)\), \((b,c)\), and \((c,a)\) provide a witness \(y\) for \(x=a\), \(x=b\), and \(x=c\). The witness is allowed to differ from \(x\), so the absence of pairs \((x,x)\) is irrelevant.
questions.hint: For each element, look for a pair of \(L\) that begins with it.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a universally quantified implication whose hypothesis is never true.
questions.question: A model has domain \(\{1,3,5\}\), and \(E(x)\) means "\(x\) is even". Is \(\forall x\,(E(x)\implies x>10)\) true in this model?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes; no element is even, so the implication holds for every element.

options.label: B
options.text: No; no element of the domain is greater than \(10\).

questions.explanation: For each element, \(E(x)\) is false, and an implication with a false hypothesis is true. So the implication holds for \(1\), \(3\), and \(5\), and the universal statement is true. This is called vacuous truth.
questions.hint: Evaluate the hypothesis of the implication for each element first.

questions.learningObjective: Find the domain in which a quantified statement about divisibility is true.
questions.question: Let \(D(x,y)\) mean "\(x\) divides \(y\)". In which domain is \(\forall x\,\forall y\,(D(x,y)\lor D(y,x))\) true?
questions.explanation: In \(\{1,2,4,8\}\) every element is a power of \(2\), so of any two elements the smaller divides the larger. In \(\{1,2,3,6\}\) the pair \(x=2\), \(y=3\) is a counterexample: neither divides the other.
questions.hint: Look for two elements of a domain such that neither divides the other.

questions.learningObjective: Decide which of two opposite quantified statements holds in a finite model.
questions.question: A model has domain \(\{1,2,3,4\}\). Which statement is true in this model?
questions.explanation: The squares of the elements are \(1\), \(4\), \(9\), and \(16\). Since \(16\ge 10\), the element \(4\) is a witness for \(\exists x\,(x^2\ge 10)\). The same element is a counterexample to \(\forall x\,(x^2<10)\); the two statements are negations of each other, so exactly one of them is true.
questions.hint: Compute the square of each element of the domain.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate two quantified statements about a relation in a finite model.
questions.question: A model has domain \(\{1,2,3\}\) and a relation \(F=\{(1,2),(2,3),(3,3)\}\). Which statement about the model is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: \(\forall x\,\exists! y\,F(x,y)\) is true, and \(\forall y\,\exists x\,F(x,y)\) is true.

options.label: B
options.text: \(\forall x\,\exists! y\,F(x,y)\) is true, and \(\forall y\,\exists x\,F(x,y)\) is false.

questions.explanation: Each of \(1\), \(2\), \(3\) is the first component of exactly one pair, so \(\forall x\,\exists! y\,F(x,y)\) is true: \(F\) is a function on the domain. For \(y=1\) there is no pair with second component \(1\), so \(\forall y\,\exists x\,F(x,y)\) is false: the function is not onto.
questions.hint: Check whether every element of the domain appears as a second component.
